blocks.content: A service is the fundamental unit inside a Compose file, one named block describing exactly one container, its image, its configuration, and how it participates in the overall stack.
Everything you would otherwise pass as flags to docker run, ports, environment variables, volumes, restart policy, lives inside that service's block in the Compose file instead.

blocks.alt: A service block replaces a docker run command's worth of flags

blocks.content: 2. A Real Stack Is Usually Several Services
blocks.text: 2. A Real Stack Is Usually Several Services

blocks.content: A typical Compose file defines multiple services side by side, an app service for your application code, a db service for the database, perhaps a cache service for Redis, each independently configured but started together.

blocks.alt: Several services, defined side by side, started together

blocks.content:
services:
  app:
    build: .
  db:
    image: postgres:15
  cache:
    image: redis:7

code.content:
services:
  app:
    build: .
  db:
    image: postgres:15
  cache:
    image: redis:7

codes.yaml:
services:
  app:
    build: .
  db:
    image: postgres:15
  cache:
    image: redis:7

blocks.content: A service either pulls an existing published image (image: postgres:15) or builds one locally from a Dockerfile (build: .), exactly the same choice you would make with plain docker run versus docker build, just declared instead of scripted.

blocks.alt: Pull an existing image, or build your own from source

blocks.content: 4. A Service Name Is Also a Hostname
blocks.text: 4. A Service Name Is Also a Hostname

blocks.content: This is one of Compose's most convenient behaviors: a service's name automatically becomes the hostname other services use to reach it, exactly the automatic DNS-by-name resolution covered in the Docker Networking module's DNS Resolution topic, Compose sets this up for you with zero extra configuration.

blocks.alt: A service name works as a hostname, automatically

blocks.content:
# Inside the "app" service, this just works:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/myapp
# "db" resolves to the db service automatically

code.content:
# Inside the "app" service, this just works:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/myapp
# "db" resolves to the db service automatically

codes.text:
# Inside the "app" service, this just works:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/myapp
# "db" resolves to the db service automatically

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A service is one named container definition, everything you would pass to docker run lives inside its block instead.
A service name doubles automatically as a hostname other services can use to reach it, no manual networking setup required.
